claim: Age is the major risk factor for mortality after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Age is the major risk factor for mortality after SARS-CoV-2 infection and older people have received priority consideration for COVID-19 vaccination.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Vaccine responses are often suboptimal in older people.
source: However, vaccine responses are often suboptimal in this age group and few people over the age of 80 years were included in vaccine registration trials.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about vaccine responses in elderly populations.

claim: Few people over the age of 80 years were included in vaccine registration trials.
source: However, vaccine responses are often suboptimal in this age group and few people over the age of 80 years were included in vaccine registration trials.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the composition of vaccine trials.

claim: Antibody responses were seen in every donor aged 80-96 years at 2 weeks after the second BNT162b2 vaccination.
source: Antibody responses were seen in every donor with high titers in 98%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study cohort of 100 people aged 80-96 years.

claim: 98% of donors aged 80-96 years had high antibody titers after the second BNT162b2 vaccination.
source: Antibody responses were seen in every donor with high titers in 98%.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study cohort.

claim: Spike-specific cellular immune responses were detectable in only 63% of donors aged 80-96 years after dual vaccination.
source: Spike-specific cellular immune responses were detectable in only 63% and correlated with humoral response.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot analysis data from the study.

claim: Spike-specific cellular immune responses correlated with humoral response in people aged 80-96 years after BNT162b2 vaccination.
source: Spike-specific cellular immune responses were detectable in only 63% and correlated with humoral response.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between ELISpot and antibody data.

claim: Previous SARS-CoV-2 infection substantially increased antibody responses after one BNT162b2 vaccine dose.
source: Previous SARS-CoV-2 infection substantially increased antibody responses after one vaccine and antibody and cellular responses remained 28-fold and 3-fold higher, respectively, after dual vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of antibody titers between previously infected and infection-naive donors.

claim: Antibody responses remained 28-fold higher in previously infected individuals after dual BNT162b2 vaccination compared to infection-naive individuals.
source: Previous SARS-CoV-2 infection substantially increased antibody responses after one vaccine and antibody and cellular responses remained 28-fold and 3-fold higher, respectively, after dual vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative comparison of antibody titers between groups.

claim: Cellular responses remained 3-fold higher in previously infected individuals after dual BNT162b2 vaccination compared to infection-naive individuals.
source: Previous SARS-CoV-2 infection substantially increased antibody responses after one vaccine and antibody and cellular responses remained 28-fold and 3-fold higher, respectively, after dual vaccination.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data comparing cellular responses between groups.

claim: Post-vaccine sera mediated strong neutralization of live Victoria infection.
source: Post-vaccine sera mediated strong neutralization of live Victoria infection and although neutralization titers were reduced 14-fold against the P.1 variant first discovered in Brazil they remained largely effective.
evidence: This is supported by live virus neutralization assay data.

claim: Neutralization titers were reduced 14-fold against the P.1 variant compared to Victoria strain.
source: Post-vaccine sera mediated strong neutralization of live Victoria infection and although neutralization titers were reduced 14-fold against the P.1 variant first discovered in Brazil they remained largely effective.
evidence: This is supported by comparative neutralization assay data between Victoria and P.1 variants.

claim: Neutralization against the P.1 variant remained largely effective despite 14-fold reduction in titers.
source: Post-vaccine sera mediated strong neutralization of live Victoria infection and although neutralization titers were reduced 14-fold against the P.1 variant first discovered in Brazil they remained largely effective.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neutralization data showing all donors maintained neutralization above ND50 of 36.

claim: The mRNA vaccine platform delivers strong humoral immunity in people up to 96 years of age.
source: These data demonstrate that the mRNA vaccine platform delivers strong humoral immunity in people up to 96 years of age and retains broad efficacy against the P.1 variant of concern.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the antibody response data across the age range studied.

claim: The BNT162b2 vaccine retains broad efficacy against the P.1 variant of concern.
source: These data demonstrate that the mRNA vaccine platform delivers strong humoral immunity in people up to 96 years of age and retains broad efficacy against the P.1 variant of concern.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the neutralization data showing maintained activity against P.1.

claim: The current COVID-19 pandemic has led to over 2.6 million deaths.
source: The current COVID-19 pandemic has led to over 2.6 million deaths but approval and widespread administration of several COVID-19 vaccine platforms have led to hope that the current pandemic may be brought under control.
evidence: This is stated as a factual statistic about the pandemic at the time of writing.

claim: It is essential that vaccine-induced immune responses are elicited effectively in people of older age for pandemic control.
source: However, in order for this to be achieved, it will be essential that vaccine-induced immune responses are elicited effectively in people of older age (Cox et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cox et al., 2020.

claim: The functional quality of immune responses deteriorates with age.
source: The functional quality of immune responses deteriorates with age and immunosenescence underlies the increased burden of infectious disease in older people as well as impaired responses to vaccine challenge (Ciabattini et al., 2018; Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciabattini et al., 2018 and Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009.

claim: Immunosenescence underlies the increased burden of infectious disease in older people.
source: The functional quality of immune responses deteriorates with age and immunosenescence underlies the increased burden of infectious disease in older people as well as impaired responses to vaccine challenge (Ciabattini et al., 2018; Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciabattini et al., 2018 and Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009.

claim: Immunosenescence underlies impaired responses to vaccine challenge in older people.
source: The functional quality of immune responses deteriorates with age and immunosenescence underlies the increased burden of infectious disease in older people as well as impaired responses to vaccine challenge (Ciabattini et al., 2018; Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ciabattini et al., 2018 and Siegrist and Aspinall, 2009.

claim: The efficacy of the annual inactivated influenza vaccine is markedly suppressed in people ≥65 years.
source: An exemplar is the efficacy of the annual inactivated influenza vaccine which is markedly suppressed in people ≥65 years (Ciabattini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ciabattini et al., 2018.

claim: Potential mechanisms underlying immune senescence include a reduction in the number of naïve T cells due to thymic involution.
source: A range of potential mechanisms may underlie the development of immune senescence, including a reduction in the number of naïve T cells due to thymic involution and accumulation of memory cells, as well as an increased serum concentration of inflammatory molecules in a phenomenon termed inflammaging (Egorov et al., 2018; Pietrobon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egorov et al., 2018 and Pietrobon et al., 2020.

claim: Potential mechanisms underlying immune senescence include accumulation of memory cells.
source: A range of potential mechanisms may underlie the development of immune senescence, including a reduction in the number of naïve T cells due to thymic involution and accumulation of memory cells, as well as an increased serum concentration of inflammatory molecules in a phenomenon termed inflammaging (Egorov et al., 2018; Pietrobon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egorov et al., 2018 and Pietrobon et al., 2020.

claim: Potential mechanisms underlying immune senescence include an increased serum concentration of inflammatory molecules in a phenomenon termed inflammaging.
source: A range of potential mechanisms may underlie the development of immune senescence, including a reduction in the number of naïve T cells due to thymic involution and accumulation of memory cells, as well as an increased serum concentration of inflammatory molecules in a phenomenon termed inflammaging (Egorov et al., 2018; Pietrobon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Egorov et al., 2018 and Pietrobon et al., 2020.

claim: Higher antigen dose is being assessed to overcome immune senescence effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
source: Approaches such as higher antigen dose, adjuvant formulation, and usage of the live inactivated vaccination are being assessed to overcome these effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
evidence: This is stated as current research approaches in the field.

claim: Adjuvant formulation is being assessed to overcome immune senescence effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
source: Approaches such as higher antigen dose, adjuvant formulation, and usage of the live inactivated vaccination are being assessed to overcome these effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
evidence: This is stated as current research approaches in the field.

claim: Usage of live inactivated vaccination is being assessed to overcome immune senescence effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
source: Approaches such as higher antigen dose, adjuvant formulation, and usage of the live inactivated vaccination are being assessed to overcome these effects and improve vaccine efficacy.
evidence: This is stated as current research approaches in the field.

claim: There is insufficient evidence to assess the potential impact of immune senescence on response to the mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines.
source: At the current time, there is insufficient evidence to assess the potential impact of immune senescence on response to the mRNA-based COVID-19 vaccines.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap at the time of the study.

claim: The nucleoside-modified RNA vaccine BNT162b2 from Pfizer BioNTech incorporating spike is strongly immunogenic.
source: The nucleoside-modified RNA vaccine BNT162b2 from Pfizer BioNTech incorporating spike (S) is strongly immunogenic but participants over the age of 75 years comprised only 4% of efficacy data (Public Health England, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Public Health England, 2021.

claim: Participants over the age of 75 years comprised only 4% of efficacy data for BNT162b2 vaccine.
source: The nucleoside-modified RNA vaccine BNT162b2 from Pfizer BioNTech incorporating spike (S) is strongly immunogenic but participants over the age of 75 years comprised only 4% of efficacy data (Public Health England, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Public Health England, 2021.

claim: The P.1 variant includes 10 mutations within the spike domain.
source: Furthermore, it is unclear if SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOC) such as the P.1 variant which includes 10 mutations within the spike domain, including N501Y, E484K, and K417T, may mediate evasion of protective immunity (Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabino et al., 2021.

claim: The P.1 variant includes the N501Y mutation.
source: Furthermore, it is unclear if SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOC) such as the P.1 variant which includes 10 mutations within the spike domain, including N501Y, E484K, and K417T, may mediate evasion of protective immunity (Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabino et al., 2021.

claim: The P.1 variant includes the E484K mutation.
source: Furthermore, it is unclear if SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOC) such as the P.1 variant which includes 10 mutations within the spike domain, including N501Y, E484K, and K417T, may mediate evasion of protective immunity (Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabino et al., 2021.

claim: The P.1 variant includes the K417T mutation.
source: Furthermore, it is unclear if SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern (VOC) such as the P.1 variant which includes 10 mutations within the spike domain, including N501Y, E484K, and K417T, may mediate evasion of protective immunity (Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabino et al., 2021.

claim: Serum samples were obtained from 98 donors at 14-21 days following the second BNT162b2 vaccine.
source: Serum samples were obtained from donors at 14–21 days following the second BNT162b2 vaccine (n=98).
evidence: This describes the study methodology and sample collection.

claim: S-specific responses were seen in all donors after BNT162b2 vaccination.
source: S-specific responses were seen in all donors with 98% above 1 in 50.
evidence: This is supported by Roche platform antibody measurement data.

claim: 98% of donors had S-specific antibody titers above 1 in 50 after BNT162b2 vaccination.
source: S-specific responses were seen in all donors with 98% above 1 in 50.
evidence: This is supported by Roche platform antibody measurement data.

claim: Two donors had low but positive S-specific antibody titers of 1 and 2.5.
source: Two donors had low but positive titers of 1 and 2.5 and antibody responses were confirmed on the MSD platform (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by MSD platform.

claim: 10% of the cohort had evidence of prior natural infection with SARS-CoV-2 based on nucleocapsid-specific antibody serostatus.
source: Nucleocapsid (N)-specific antibody serostatus was used to determine if donors had evidence of prior natural infection with SARS-CoV-2. This was seen in 10% of the cohort (10/98), with only 4 of these having reported previous symptoms indicating a high asymptomatic infection rate in this elderly cohort.
evidence: This is supported by nucleocapsid antibody testing data.

claim: Only 4 of 10 donors with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had reported previous symptoms, indicating a high asymptomatic infection rate in this elderly cohort.
source: This was seen in 10% of the cohort (10/98), with only 4 of these having reported previous symptoms indicating a high asymptomatic infection rate in this elderly cohort.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of serological evidence and symptom reporting.

claim: Donors with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had a median S-specific antibody titer of 32,250.
source: Donors with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had a median S-specific antibody titer of 32,250 which was 28-fold higher than the value of 1138 in those without prior infection (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative antibody measurement data comparing groups.

claim: Donors without prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had a median S-specific antibody titer of 1138.
source: Donors with prior SARS-CoV-2 infection had a median S-specific antibody titer of 32,250 which was 28-fold higher than the value of 1138 in those without prior infection (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative antibody measurement data.

claim: No correlation was seen between nucleocapsid titer and spike-specific titer amongst those with evidence of previous infection.
source: No correlation was seen between the nucleocapsid titer and spike-specific titer amongst those with evidence of previous infection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Very strong correlation was seen between values obtained from serum Roche anti-S ELISA and values from DBS eluates (r=0.68; p<0.0001).
source: Very strong correlation was seen between values obtained from serum Roche anti-S ELISA and values from DBS eluates (r=0.68; p<0.0001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between two measurement platforms shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Antibody responses were detectable by DBS in 63% of samples after the first vaccine.
source: Antibody responses were detectable by DBS in 63% of samples after the first vaccine (55/88) and this rose to 96% when samples were taken after the second vaccine administration (91/95).
evidence: This is supported by DBS measurement data after first vaccination.

claim: Antibody responses were detectable by DBS in 96% of samples after the second vaccine.
source: Antibody responses were detectable by DBS in 63% of samples after the first vaccine (55/88) and this rose to 96% when samples were taken after the second vaccine administration (91/95).
evidence: This is supported by DBS measurement data after second vaccination.

claim: Amongst those previously infected with SARS-CoV-2, only a 6% rise in the antibody ratio was demonstrated between the first and second vaccines.
source: Amongst those previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 only a 6% rise in the antibody ratio was demonstrated between the first and second vaccines, suggesting minimal additional benefit from booster vaccination (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by DBS data comparing first and second vaccine responses in previously infected individuals shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The minimal increase in antibody response between first and second vaccines in previously infected individuals suggests minimal additional benefit from booster vaccination.
source: Amongst those previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 only a 6% rise in the antibody ratio was demonstrated between the first and second vaccines, suggesting minimal additional benefit from booster vaccination (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the small increase in antibody levels after the second dose.

claim: Amongst donors with no evidence of previous natural infection, a 3.1-fold increase in the antibody ratio was observed between the first and second vaccines.
source: Amongst donors with no evidence of previous natural infection, a 3.1-fold increase in the ratio was observed between the first and second vaccines (median 1.2 [IQR 0.7–1.7] vs. 3.8 [IQR 2.8–4.7]; p=<0.0001 paired t-test [Figure 1E]).
evidence: This is supported by paired comparison of DBS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Spike-specific T cell responses were detectable above threshold values in 63% of participants (62/98).
source: Spike-specific T cell responses were detectable above threshold values in 63% of participants (62/98) and responses against the S1 and S2 domains were equivalent (32 vs. 28 spots/million peripheral blood mononuclear cell [PBMC], respectively; p=0.35) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by IFN-γ ELISpot analysis data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Responses against the S1 and S2 spike domains were equivalent (32 vs. 28 spots/million PBMC, respectively; p=0.35).
source: Spike-specific T cell responses were detectable above threshold values in 63% of participants (62/98) and responses against the S1 and S2 domains were equivalent (32 vs. 28 spots/million peripheral blood mononuclear cell [PBMC], respectively; p=0.35) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by comparative ELISpot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The median magnitude of total spike-specific T cell response was 84 spots/million PBMC (IQR 6–55).
source: The median magnitude of total spike-specific response was 84 spots/million PBMC (IQR 6–55) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Cellular responses against nucleocapsid were significantly greater in those with prior infection (N median 28 vs. 4 spots/million; p<0.0001).
source: As expected, cellular responses against N were significantly greater in those with prior infection (N median 28 vs. 4 spots/million; p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data comparing previously infected and infection-naive groups.

claim: Previously infected individuals developed threefold stronger T cell responses against spike peptides after vaccination (228 spots/million PBMC) compared to uninfected people (72 spots/million PBMC; p=0.0033).
source: Interestingly, this group also developed threefold stronger T cell responses against spike peptides after vaccination (228 spots/million PBMC) compared to uninfected people (72 spots/million PBMC; p=0.0033) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by comparative ELISpot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: An increased cellular response against the nucleocapsid protein was observed in people with previous natural infection compared to those who were uninfected (median N response of 12 spots/million vs. 4; p=0.0049).
source: Similarly, an increased cellular response against the nucleocapsid and membrane proteins was also observed in people with previous natural infection and those who were uninfected (median N response of 12 spots/million for those with previous infection vs. 4 for those with infection naïve; p=0.0049 and for M response, amongst those previous exposed, a median of 28 spots/million compared to 4 p≤0.0001) (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: An increased cellular response against the membrane protein was observed in people with previous natural infection compared to those who were uninfected (median M response of 28 spots/million vs. 4; p≤0.0001).
source: Similarly, an increased cellular response against the nucleocapsid and membrane proteins was also observed in people with previous natural infection and those who were uninfected (median N response of 12 spots/million for those with previous infection vs. 4 for those with infection naïve; p=0.0049 and for M response, amongst those previous exposed, a median of 28 spots/million compared to 4 p≤0.0001) (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Spike-specific antibody and T cell responses after vaccination were correlated (r=0.46; p=0.000003).
source: Finally, we determined the relationship between the spike-specific antibody and T cell responses after vaccination and found these to be correlated (r=0.46; p=0.000003) (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No correlation between age and humoral responses against spike protein was observed in people aged 80-96 years.
source: Although our cohort contained people up to 96 years of age no correlation between age and humoral or cellular responses were observed against the spike protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: No correlation between age and cellular responses against spike protein was observed in people aged 80-96 years.
source: Although our cohort contained people up to 96 years of age no correlation between age and humoral or cellular responses were observed against the spike protein (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: BNT162b2 vaccination elicits robust immunity even at extreme older age.
source: As such these data demonstrate clearly that BNT162b2 vaccination elicits robust immunity even at extreme older age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of age-related decline in responses within the 80-96 year age range.

claim: Median ND50 was 2578 against the Victoria strain.
source: Median ND50 was 2578 against the Victoria strain with almost all samples falling between 1000 and 15,895 (n=23).
evidence: This is supported by live virus neutralization assay data.

claim: Almost all samples had ND50 values between 1000 and 15,895 against the Victoria strain.
source: Median ND50 was 2578 against the Victoria strain with almost all samples falling between 1000 and 15,895 (n=23).
evidence: This is supported by live virus neutralization assay data.

claim: ND50 values for neutralization of the P.1 variant were reduced by 14-fold to a median value of 180.
source: ND50 values for neutralization of the P.1 variant were reduced by 14-fold to a median value of 180 but remained above 36 for all donors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by comparative neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ND50 values for neutralization of the P.1 variant remained above 36 for all donors.
source: ND50 values for neutralization of the P.1 variant were reduced by 14-fold to a median value of 180 but remained above 36 for all donors (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by neutralization assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Overall anti-S IgG titer correlated strongly with neutralizing activity against Victoria (r=0.857, p<0.0001).
source: As anticipated, overall anti-S IgG titer correlated strongly with neutralizing activity (Victoria r=0.857, p<0.0001; Brazil r=0.796, p<0.0001) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Overall anti-S IgG titer correlated strongly with neutralizing activity against P.1 variant (r=0.796, p<0.0001).
source: As anticipated, overall anti-S IgG titer correlated strongly with neutralizing activity (Victoria r=0.857, p<0.0001; Brazil r=0.796, p<0.0001) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Spike-specific antibody responses after BNT162b2 vaccination typically exceeded those seen after natural infection.
source: We detected spike-specific antibody responses in all older people which typically exceeded those seen after natural infection (Krutikov et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from Krutikov et al., 2021.

claim: The findings likely underlie the excellent clinical protection emerging from vaccine trials with 94% protection from symptomatic infection in a real-world setting.
source: It is likely that these findings underlie the excellent clinical protection that is emerging from vaccine trials in this population with 94% protection from symptomatic infection in a real-world setting and 89% efficacy in people over 80 years of age (Dagan et al., 2021; Bernal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study findings to clinical efficacy data from Dagan et al., 2021 and Bernal et al., 2021.

claim: BNT162b2 vaccine shows 89% efficacy in people over 80 years of age.
source: It is likely that these findings underlie the excellent clinical protection that is emerging from vaccine trials in this population with 94% protection from symptomatic infection in a real-world setting and 89% efficacy in people over 80 years of age (Dagan et al., 2021; Bernal et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dagan et al., 2021 and Bernal et al., 2021.

claim: Antibody responses remained robust in donors up to 96 years of age.
source: A striking feature was that antibody responses remained robust in donors up to 96 years of age, indicating that mRNA vaccine efficacy for induction of humoral responses appears essentially independent of age within this older population.
evidence: This is supported by the lack of age-related decline in antibody responses in the study data.

claim: mRNA vaccine efficacy for induction of humoral responses appears essentially independent of age within the 80-96 year old population.
source: A striking feature was that antibody responses remained robust in donors up to 96 years of age, indicating that mRNA vaccine efficacy for induction of humoral responses appears essentially independent of age within this older population.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of correlation between age and antibody responses.

claim: T cell responses were present in 63% of people but were of relatively low magnitude.
source: In contrast, the induction of spike-specific cellular responses was less complete. T cell responses were present in 63% of people but were of relatively low magnitude.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data showing the proportion and magnitude of T cell responses.

claim: The S1 and S2 spike domains were equivalently immunodominant.
source: The S1 and S2 domains were equivalently immunodominant.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data showing similar responses to both domains.

claim: Undetectable or very low cellular responses were seen in 37% of people.
source: However, it is noteworthy that undetectable or very low cellular responses were seen in 37% of people.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data showing the proportion without detectable responses.

claim: A strong correlation was seen between the magnitude of cellular and humoral immunity as observed in natural infection.
source: Indeed, a strong correlation was seen between the magnitude of the cellular and humoral immunity as observed in natural infection (Zuo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by correlation data in the study and comparison with Zuo et al., 2021.

claim: Salvagno et al. reported spike-specific antibody responses of 1364 U/ml with the same assay.
source: Of note, Salvagno et al. reported spike-specific antibody responses of 1364 U/ml with the same assay, which is comparable, although somewhat higher, to the value of 1138 seen in our study (Salvagno et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with data from Salvagno et al., 2021.

claim: No participants with a history of previous natural infection had suboptimal cellular immunity.
source: Indeed, no participants with a history of previous natural infection had suboptimal cellular immunity compared to 44% in uninfected donors.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data comparing previously infected and infection-naive groups.

claim: 44% of uninfected donors had suboptimal cellular immunity.
source: Indeed, no participants with a history of previous natural infection had suboptimal cellular immunity compared to 44% in uninfected donors.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data from infection-naive donors.

claim: Strong responses were observed after only the first vaccine dose in previously infected individuals, with no significant increment after the second dose when administered with a 3-week interval.
source: Interestingly, we also observed strong responses after only the first vaccine dose in this group, with no significant increment after the second dose when administered with a 3-week interval.
evidence: This is supported by DBS data comparing first and second dose responses in previously infected individuals.

claim: These findings are comparable with those seen in healthcare workers which have led to suggestions that a single vaccine delivery may be sufficient for those with prior natural infection.
source: As such these findings are comparable with those seen in healthcare workers which have led to suggestions that a single vaccine delivery may be sufficient for those with prior natural infection (Levi et al., 2021; Krammer et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Levi et al., 2021 and Krammer et al., 2021.

claim: Strong neutralization of the Victoria strain correlated with global spike-specific response.
source: The optimal in vitro correlation of natural protection is assessment of live virus neutralization and strong neutralization of the Victoria strain correlated with global spike-specific response.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between antibody titers and neutralization data.

claim: The P.1 VOC contains a range of mutations within the spike domain including E484K which can mediate escape from recognition by some antibodies.
source: The P.1 VOC contains a range of mutations within the spike domain including E484K which can mediate escape from recognition by some antibodies (Sabino et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sabino et al., 2021.

claim: A 14-fold reduction in median neutralization titer was observed with the P.1 variant, which is larger than a 6.7-fold decrease in 30 younger vaccinees using pseudo-neutralization assays.
source: A pronounced 14-fold reduction in median neutralization titer was observed with this variant which is larger than a 6.7-fold decrease in 30 younger vaccinees using pseudo-neutralization assays (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021) and a 3.8–4.8-fold decrease with the use of live virus (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison of the study findings with data from Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021.

claim: A 3.8-4.8-fold decrease in neutralization of P.1 variant was observed with the use of live virus in other studies.
source: A pronounced 14-fold reduction in median neutralization titer was observed with this variant which is larger than a 6.7-fold decrease in 30 younger vaccinees using pseudo-neutralization assays (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021) and a 3.8–4.8-fold decrease with the use of live virus (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with data from Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Neutralizing activity remained somewhat robust across the cohort suggesting that vaccinated older people are unlikely to be highly susceptible to the P.1 variant.
source: It is currently unclear how neutralization titers in vitro correlate with clinical protection but neutralizing activity remained somewhat robust across the cohort suggesting that vaccinated older people are unlikely to be highly susceptible to this rapidly emerging variant.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the maintained neutralization activity above threshold levels.

claim: 100 participants aged 80 years or older were recruited who were living in community dwellings, able to attend a vaccination center, and did not require assistance with daily living or self-care.
source: 100 participants, aged 80 years or older, were recruited who were in living in community dwellings, able to attend a vaccination center, and did not require assistance with daily living or self-care.
evidence: This describes the study population and inclusion criteria.

claim: The median age of participants was 84 years (IQR 80–87 or range 80–96).
source: The median age of participants was 84 years (IQR 80–87 or range 80–96) and 58% were female.
evidence: This describes the demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: 58% of participants were female.
source: The median age of participants was 84 years (IQR 80–87 or range 80–96) and 58% were female.
evidence: This describes the demographic characteristics of the study cohort.

claim: All participants received the Pfizer BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine with a 3-week interval between the first and second doses.
source: All participants received the Pfizer BNT162b2 COVID-19 vaccine with a 3-week interval between the first and second doses.
evidence: This describes the vaccination protocol used in the study.

claim: A phlebotomy sample was taken at 2 weeks following the second vaccine.
source: A phlebotomy sample was taken at 2 weeks following the second vaccine.
evidence: This describes the sample collection timing.

claim: A finger prick DBS sample was taken at 3 weeks following the first vaccination in 88 donors.
source: A finger prick DBS sample was also taken at 3 weeks following the first vaccination in 88 donors and at 2 weeks following the second vaccination (Morley et al., 2020).
